Description: Check weather and monsoon/storm advisories for the specific week, not just the season.
Register with local tourism office / forest department where required before entering core zones.
Carry printed copies of ID, permits, and emergency contacts — do not rely only on phone storage.
Inform a family member or friend of the exact itinerary, stops, and expected return date.
Download offline maps and emergency content before leaving network coverage.
Carry a basic first-aid kit: antiseptic, bandages, anti-allergy tablets, ORS packets, personal prescriptions.
Carry mosquito repellent; consult a doctor about malaria prophylaxis for multi-day trips.
Fully charge your phone and carry a power bank — charging is unreliable at remote homestays.
Carry a physical whistle as a no-battery way to signal for help.
Note the last point of network signal on your route before it drops.
Keep at least one person in the group aware of exact real-time location, even without signal.
Never split up in a no-network zone, even for a few minutes.
Identify the nearest facility (health post/police/forest office) immediately upon arrival at each new stop.
Keep local emergency contacts (boatman, guide, homestay host) saved digitally and written on paper as backup.
Avoid risky photography spots (cliff edges, riverbanks, close wildlife shots) — many trip injuries come from photo-taking, not the 'expected' hazards.
Wear closed, ankle-covering footwear at all times outside the boat.
Keep the person still, keep the bite area below heart level. Do NOT cut or suck the wound. Move toward help calmly but immediately.
Do not attempt to self-treat a suspected fracture — immobilize the area and prioritize evacuation.
Get to the nearest solid shelter immediately — do not wait to finish the current activity or boat ride.
Stay in place rather than wandering further. Use whistle signals. Activate any available offline SOS feature.
Know in advance whether your situation needs the nearest primary health center or requires direct evacuation to a larger hospital.
Confirm boat departure/return timing with the boatman directly — schedules here are tide-based, not fixed-clock.
Avoid walking near creek edges or watchtower peripheries alone — crocodile proximity increases in monsoon.
Maintain distance from the watchtower's creek-facing edge — known crocodile basking area directly below.
Never step off the marked wooden plank path near the canopy walk — pneumatophores (sharp mangrove roots) are a real trip/injury hazard.
This stop is strictly tide-dependent — confirm return timing before starting the canopy walk, not after.
Build in extra buffer time — this is the farthest core stop, and a tide miscalculation risks a long stranded wait.
Avoid the overgrown ruins-adjacent areas — known snake habitat, especially after rain.
Confirm private/shared vehicle arrangements in advance if combining road and boat access.
Note this is the last point with reliable network before the forest zones — send any pending messages here.
Jetty paths can be slippery after rain — take care during homestay arrival/departure.
Boat-only access here means tide timing directly affects arrival and departure — confirm before planning a sunset visit.
Reconfirm your boat departure slot here, since it's tide-scheduled and the main organized departure point for tours.
This is a well-known point of route confusion (five converging channels) — never let the boat separate from a known, licensed boatman here.
This open confluence is highly exposed to sudden wind/weather shifts — avoid lingering here if a storm is forecast.
